Writhing describes something — usually a living creature, or something that moves like one — that is twisting, curling, and contorting continuously in an uncontrolled, restless way. The movement is not clean or purposeful. It is messy, repeated, and often desperate.

Think of a worm you've placed on the ground. It doesn't just sit still or move in a straight line — it bends, coils, and squirms in every direction at once. That is writhing.
What makes "writhing" different from just "moving" or "twisting"?

Three things set it apart:

  1. It's continuous. A writhing thing doesn't twist once and stop. It keeps going — over and over, without settling.
  2. It's uncontrolled. The movement isn't graceful or deliberate. It's the kind of movement that happens to something, not by something with calm intention.
  3. It suggests suffering or intense sensation. Most of the time, something writhes because of something — pain, extreme discomfort, fear, or powerful emotion. The word carries that weight.
Who or what can be writhing?

People in pain:

The writhing patient was rushed into the emergency room.

Here, the patient is twisting and contorting uncontrollably because of intense physical pain. You can picture someone who cannot lie still, cannot find a comfortable position, turning and curling and bending involuntarily.

Animals:

A writhing snake lay tangled in the net.

A snake's natural movement is already sinuous (wavy and coiling), so "writhing" amplifies that — suggesting it is in distress, struggling, unable to get free.

A mass or crowd of living things:

The fisherman pulled up a net full of writhing fish.

When many creatures are packed together and all moving in that squirming, contorting way, "writhing" captures that disturbing, chaotic energy perfectly.

"Writhing" can also describe non-living things that look like they are twisting and contorting — particularly things that move in a sinuous, restless way:

Writhing flames shot out of the broken window.

Fire doesn't feel pain, but its curling, twisting, and unpredictable movement resembles writhing. Writers use this to make descriptions feel alive, intense, and even threatening.

Writhing vines covered the ancient wall.

Here, the vines aren't literally moving, but their twisted, coiling shape looks like the frozen image of something that was writhing. Used this way, the word paints a visual of something dense, tangled, and organic.

When used about a person, writhing almost always implies deep, involuntary suffering. It is a strong, vivid word. It tells you the person is not just uncomfortable — they are in the grip of something powerful that their body is fighting against or reacting to.

It can also occasionally describe emotional or mental anguish:

He was a writhing mess of guilt and regret.

This is figurative — it means his guilt was so intense and unrelenting that it felt like physical torture, something squirming and uncontrollable inside him.
How it compares to similar words

WordWhat it emphasizes
  • Squirming is similar but slightly milder and often used for smaller creatures or for social discomfort (e.g., a child squirming in their seat out of boredom). Writhing is more intense.
  • Twisting is a neutral description of a single motion. Writhing is continuous, involuntary twisting — with suffering implied.
  • Contorting focuses on the extreme bending of a shape. Writhing is more about the relentless, ongoing, uncontrolled nature of the movement.
  • Wriggling suggests a small, quick, almost playful movement (like a puppy). Writhing is heavier and more serious.
A quick summary to lock it in

Writhing = continuously twisting and contorting in an uncontrolled, restless way, usually driven by pain, suffering, or powerful sensation.

It is a word that makes you see something struggling, unable to be still, caught in the grip of something it cannot escape. When you read it, picture a worm on a hot surface, a person clutching their stomach and unable to hold still, or a mass of snakes tangled together — all twisting, turning, never at rest. That image is writhing.
